design_detail: Analysis of an international online survey of people who had drunk ayahuasca at least once, run 2017 to 2019 in English, Portuguese, Spanish, German, Italian and Czech, with non-random recruitment through organizations, retreat centres, ayahuasca churches, online groups and forums, Facebook and conference flyers, no incentive, and University of Melbourne ethics approval (1545143.3). Of 10,836 respondents, the 6,877 who had drunk ayahuasca with two or fewer groups were analysed. Exposures, all self-reported: context of the last drink (ayahuasca church, traditional shaman, or other); motivations (15 checkboxes in three factor scores); ceremony characteristics present in the last context (counts of traditional and non-traditional practices; religious hymns or sermons); a 1 to 4 rating of support and safety and a 1 to 4 rating of preparation activities; additional supports offered outside ceremonies at the place of drinking (religious or spiritual counselling, psychologist or psychotherapist, yoga or tai-chi, fasting); and drinking mostly in a traditional Amazonian country other than Brazil. Outcomes: intermediate (self-insights, Short Index of Mystical Orientation, a single spiritual-significance item, extreme fear or panic during a session, integration difficulties in the weeks or months after, closeness of a drinking community) and final (perceived growth in psychological wellbeing, SF-12 mental component score, Kessler-10, and, for 1,278 people with anxiety or depression diagnosed when they drank, the Patient Global Impression of Change). Linear and stereotype logistic regressions after multiple imputation (20 data sets), adjusted for age, sex, university education, number of lifetime mental-health diagnoses, number of times drunk and years since the last drink, then a generalized structural equation model built iteratively on the same data. Rated with ROBINS-E.
can_establish: How ceremony practices, support and preparation ratings, additional supports and motivations differed between church, traditional-shaman and other contexts among 6,877 self-selected people who drink ayahuasca, and which of them went with these people's retrospective ratings of the acute experience and of later difficulties, and with their current mental health, after adjustment for a few demographic and drinking-history variables.
cannot_establish: That any ceremony feature, support, preparation activity or fasting changes the acute experience or mental health (one cross-sectional, self-selected, self-report survey with no measure taken before ayahuasca, exposures rated retrospectively by the people who rated the outcomes, and a path model selected on the same data); the dose, composition or purity of what was drunk (not measured); or how often frightening experiences or later difficulties occur among people who drink ayahuasca generally.

sample.recruitment: Online survey 2017 to 2019 in six languages, promoted through websites and email invitations from relevant organizations, ayahuasca retreat centres and churches, online groups and forums, Facebook, and flyers at conferences and events; no financial incentive; suspected duplicates removed and partly completed surveys kept (Materials and Methods › Study Design, 1st paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 or over, with at least one use of ayahuasca. For this paper only respondents who had drunk with two or fewer groups were included (6,877 of 10,836); the reason for the restriction is not stated.
sample.demographics: By last context (church, traditional, other; Table 3): women 50.7%, 48.5%, 50.6%; mean age 40.0, 40.3 and 38.4 years; university education 63.2%, 60.4%, 61.3%; living in Brazil 87.0%, 6.4%, 19.4%, in Europe 4.8%, 41.5%, 41.0%, in North America 6.8%, 31.9%, 22.2%; any lifetime mental-health diagnosis 29.2%, 39.0%, 44.5%; ayahuasca drunk more than 200 times 56.8%, 0.3%, 1.1%, and 5 times or fewer 7.1%, 66.0%, 68.0% (editors' sums of Table 3 rows); years since the last drink 1.2, 1.6 and 1.2.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single survey). Item non-response is visible in Table 3 (for example, lifetime mental-health diagnoses answered by 5,524 of the 6,817 with a known context) and was handled by multiple imputation; the amount missing per variable is not otherwise reported.
sample.selection_effects: Non-random, self-selected sample recruited largely through ayahuasca organizations, retreat centres and churches; the authors state that it risks a bias towards people who had positive effects (Discussion, 8th paragraph). People who were harmed or who stopped drinking may be under-represented. The unexplained restriction to people who drank with two or fewer groups removed 37% of respondents (editors' calculation). Church members are half of the sample and differ sharply from the others in country, number of times drunk and mental-health history.

exposure.measurement: All self-reported in one online survey. Context of the last drink: a ceremony with one or more traditional shamans; the UDV, Santo Daime or Barquinha churches; or other (non-traditional, mixed, no guide or no ceremony). Motivations: 15 checkboxes summed in three factors from an exploratory factor analysis, therapeutic (0 to 6), self-knowledge (0 to 4) and experiential (0 to 5). Ceremony characteristics present in the last context: traditional (0 to 6: live icaros, recommended sexual abstinence before ceremonies, blowing of smoke, individual blessings, whistling, sucking from affected parts of the body), non-traditional (0 to 5: smudging, other live singing, non-traditional instruments, recitations, dance) and religious hymns or sermons (yes or no). Two ratings of the respondent's experience of the last context, 1 (not at all) to 4 (very much): support and safety (mean of 4 items: empathy, respect and genuineness of those leading; emotional and physical safety in the ceremony space; availability of support during the ceremony; a sense of the ceremony as a powerful and sacred ritual) and preparation activities (mean of 2 items: a chance to discuss one's history, motivations or concerns before drinking; guidance before drinking about dealing with possible difficulties). Additional supports provided outside ceremonies at the place of drinking (yes or no): religious or spiritual counselling, a psychologist or psychotherapist session, yoga or tai-chi, fasting. Most drinking in Peru, Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia or Venezuela (Brazil excluded) coded as a traditional country.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Dose, concentration, quantity and composition of the brew were not measured (Discussion, 8th paragraph). Lifetime number of times drunk was recorded in 10 categories (from 1 to 500–5000) and entered as a covariate, as were years since the last drink.
exposure.polysubstance: Not measured or adjusted in this paper; alcohol and other drug use from the same survey is analysed in a companion paper (Perkins et al., 2021, cited for the list of self-insights).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable. Current mental health (SF-12, K10) was measured at the survey, a mean of 1.2 to 1.6 years after the last drink (Table 3).

comparison.controls: No group without ayahuasca. Comparisons are among people who drink ayahuasca: across contexts and regions (Tables 2 and 3), and by levels of each motivation, ceremony, support and country variable, each adjusted for the others and for the covariates (Tables 4 and 5).
comparison.matching: None; regression adjustment for age (decades), sex, university education, number of lifetime mental-health diagnoses, number of times drunk (the category entered as a single term) and years since the last drink, with all exposure variables entered together.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Mental health before any ayahuasca use (proxied only by the number of lifetime diagnoses, whose timing relative to ayahuasca is unknown; the authors call the proxy not completely satisfactory), personality, state of mind when drinking (the authors note that set was limited to motivations), dose and composition, other drug use, and the facilitators' skill (proxied by country).

outcomes.instruments: Intermediate: number of self-insights (7 listed insights, alpha 0.80); the Short Index of Mystical Orientation (9 items rated 1 to 10, total 9 to 90, with 'god' replaced by 'god/spirit/the divine'), used for the intensity of mystical experience during the acute phase; the spirituality item of the Persisting Effects Questionnaire (PEQ-S: one six-point item, from not at all significant to the single most spiritually significant experience of one's life); extreme fear or panic during the ayahuasca session (one item, 0 to 10); number of integration difficulties in the weeks or months after drinking (PHQ-4 plus 5 items such as feeling disconnected or alone, or disturbing thoughts, feelings or sensations); closeness of a community one drinks with (4 points). Final: perceived growth in psychological wellbeing (PWG; Psychological Well-Being Post-Traumatic Changes Questionnaire, 18 items on 5 points); SF-12 mental component score (0 to 100, higher better) and Kessler-10 (10 to 50, higher more distress), both current; the Patient Global Impression of Change (6 points, from much worsened to completely improved) for anxiety or depression diagnosed when drinking ayahuasca on any occasion.
outcomes.validity_norms: SF-12 and K10 are standard measures of current status and, as the authors note, not retrospective. The PWB-PTCQ was developed for change after trauma. The Short Index of Mystical Orientation's source, by the title in the reference list, is a study of mystical orientation among Roman Catholic priests, and no validation for rating an acute ayahuasca experience is reported. The spirituality, fear and community measures are single items and the self-insight and integration counts are new; no validation is reported for them.
outcomes.operationalization: A difficult experience is extreme fear or panic during a session (one item) and integration difficulties in the weeks or months after; a good one is self-insights, mystical and spiritual ratings and community closeness. All were rated by the respondent at the survey, retrospectively, for an occasion that is not always specified (the exposures refer to the last context); none was measured before drinking. Which outcomes were modelled by stereotype logistic rather than linear regression is not stated.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 130 counts the coefficients of the 13 non-covariate predictors across the 6 intermediate (Table 4) and 4 final (Table 5) outcomes; Table 2 adds 30 tests of differences by context and region, and the path model further tests.

analysis.effect_sizes: Unstandardized coefficients B (SE) with p values; no R-squared, standardized coefficients or intervals (the 95% intervals below are B ± 1.96 SE, editors' calculation). Support and safety (1 to 4): extreme fear −0.29 (−0.43 to −0.15), integration difficulties −0.13 (−0.23 to −0.03), K10 −0.62 (−0.86 to −0.38), SF-12 MCS 1.5 (1.05 to 1.95), PWG 1.91 (1.42 to 2.40), SIMO 2.42 (1.60 to 3.24), PGIC 0.07 (p = 0.181). Preparation activities (1 to 4): integration difficulties −0.14 (−0.20 to −0.08), extreme fear −0.01 (p = 0.816), K10 −0.25 (−0.39 to −0.11), SF-12 MCS 0.45 (0.18 to 0.72), PWG 0.75 (0.48 to 1.02), PGIC 0.13 (0.07 to 0.19). Fasting: SIMO 1.69 (0.44 to 2.94), PWG 0.97 (0.24 to 1.70), no other association. Traditional practices: extreme fear 0.18 (0.12 to 0.24), K10 0.16 (0.04 to 0.28). Drinking mostly in a traditional country: extreme fear 0.7 (0.43 to 0.97), K10 −0.47 (−0.90 to −0.04). Religious characteristics: extreme fear −0.38 (−0.56 to −0.20). Therapeutic motivation: extreme fear 0.21 (0.15 to 0.27), integration difficulties 0.15 (0.11 to 0.19), K10 0.43 (0.33 to 0.53). For scale: across the whole 1 to 4 range of either rating, the adjusted difference in current distress is under 2 points of the K10's 40-point span (editors' arithmetic). Path coefficients of the structural model are only in Figure 2 (an image) and supplementary Table S1 (not read).
analysis.covariates: Age (decades), female sex, university education, number of lifetime mental-health diagnoses, number of times drunk and years since the last drink; all exposures entered together; multiple imputation by chained equations (20 data sets) for all model variables; multicollinearity checked (VIF above 3, correlations above 0.7: none).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned. The structural model was selected by iteratively adding or removing paths using the regression results, theoretical justification, path significance and information criteria (Materials and Methods › Statistical Analysis, 3rd paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Tables 4 and 5 print every coefficient, which limits selective reporting within the regressions. The structural model, selected on the same data, is presented in the abstract as verifying the relationships. The discussion's summaries depart from the tables in two places (reporting issue 4).
analysis.power: Not addressed. With 6,877 respondents very small coefficients reach significance; the authors note that many effects were small individually (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among self-selected people who drink ayahuasca, half of them church members mostly in Brazil and most of the rest people who had drunk a few times in traditional or other contexts, higher ratings of support and safety at the last ceremony, and of preparation activities, went with fewer reported integration difficulties, more self-insights and higher spiritual ratings, more perceived growth in wellbeing and slightly better current mental health; support and safety, but not preparation, also went with less reported extreme fear. Traditional practices, drinking mostly in a traditional Amazonian country, non-traditional practices and therapeutic motivation went with more reported extreme fear, and religious church characteristics with less. Fasting and yoga or tai-chi went with higher mystical and wellbeing-growth ratings. The adjusted differences are small: under 2 K10 points across the full range of either rating.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says a structural model was used to verify the relationships, the methods describe that model as a network of causal relationships, and the conclusion states that aspects of setting and set "appear to have significant effects" on acute experiences, integration difficulties and longer-term mental health (Discussion, 10th paragraph), singling out supports giving a sense of safety and preparation activities as especially important. Gaps: (1) causal and verification language from one cross-sectional survey, with a path model chosen on the same data; (2) the support-and-safety rating is the respondent's own retrospective judgment of the ceremony, near the top of its scale (means 3.4 to 3.9 of 4), and contains items close to the outcomes (feeling safe in the ceremony space versus extreme fear; a powerful and sacred ritual versus spiritual significance), so the association can run from the experience to the rating; (3) there is no measure of mental health before ayahuasca and no dose information, both acknowledged; (4) the discussion overstates two table results (reporting issue 4). Against this, the authors state the main limitations (self-selection favouring positive experiences, self-report, retrospective items, no pre-use mental health, no dose data), note that many effects were small, and conclude that no one set of practices was shown to be superior.

timeline.event: Haijen et al. prospective study of predictors of responses to psychedelics, cited for the role of set and setting

Russ et al. on states and traits related to psychedelic experiences, cited for the point that mental state at ingestion predicts mystical and adverse experiences, which this survey did not measure (as cited).

Sarris et al. international cross-sectional study of 11,912 ayahuasca consumers on depression and anxiety, from an overlapping author group, cited for number of uses as a strong predictor of outcomes (as cited; how its sample relates to this paper's 10,836 respondents is not explained).
Perkins et al. companion paper on alcohol and drug use from the same survey (as cited; the reference-list entry lacks journal and DOI; on this project's DMT-Ayahuasca list, not read here).

Bouso et al. on adverse effects of ayahuasca from the Global Ayahuasca Survey, with overlapping authors (on this project's DMT-Ayahuasca list; not read here, so whether its data overlap with this paper's was not checked).
Perkins et al. on ayahuasca use in naturalistic settings and mental health and wellbeing in a large global dataset (on this project's DMT-Ayahuasca list; not read here).

replication.where_it_stands: No independent replication. Companion and later papers from overlapping authors appear to draw on the same survey and must not be counted as independent support. Studies of set and setting in ayahuasca ceremonies and retreats on this project's DMT-Ayahuasca list (Uthaug et al., 2021; Pontual et al., 2022), not read for this card, are the next comparisons; the question whether support, preparation or fasting changes the experience needs measures taken before and soon after ceremonies.

funding.funder: As printed: JS is supported by an NHMRC Clinical Research Fellowship (APP1125000) (Funding). No other funding of the survey is stated.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: the authors declare that the research was conducted without commercial or financial relationships that could be construed as a potential conflict of interest (Conflict of Interest).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of Melbourne (the first author coordinated the study and designed and ran the analysis), an independent researcher in Melbourne, the University of Campinas (ICARO), ICEERS (Barcelona) with Universitat Rovira i Virgili and the University of São Paulo, Mendel University in Brno, the Federal University of Rio Grande do Norte, and Western Sydney University (NICM) with the Melbourne Clinic. Data are not shared: participants' consent limited access to the research team. Several supporting works cited are by the authors (Sarris et al., 2021; Perkins et al., 2021; Horák and Verter, 2019). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people booked into ayahuasca ceremonies of different kinds that measures mental health, expectations and state of mind before the ceremony, records what was drunk where possible, has setting and support rated independently by observers as well as by participants, and rates the acute experience (fear, challenging and mystical experience) within a day and mental health at follow-up, against pre-specified hypotheses; where retreats already differ in preparation, a cluster-randomized comparison of a standard preparation session would test preparation directly.

domains.note: Adjusted for age, sex, education, number of lifetime diagnoses, number of times drunk and years since the last drink, but not for mental health before ayahuasca, personality, state of mind, dose or other drug use; number of times drunk, entered as one term across ten categories, cannot remove the very large difference in experience between church members and the others.

For the support-and-safety and preparation ratings, the exposures the paper emphasizes: retrospective self-ratings of the last ceremony, near the ceiling, with items overlapping the outcomes in content and open to being shaped by how the experience went. The yes-or-no supports (fasting, yoga, counselling) are less exposed to this and would be judged high. Exposures refer to the last context, while several outcomes refer to unspecified or earlier occasions; motivations have no stated reference time.

Self-selected through organizations, retreat centres and churches, with a likely bias towards positive experiences that the authors acknowledge; 37% of respondents removed by an unexplained restriction to two or fewer groups.

Later ceremonies, integration work and therapy between the last drink and the survey (a mean of 1.2 to 1.6 years) are not recorded; the number of times drunk, adjusted for, is partly a consequence of earlier experiences.

Multiple imputation (20 data sets) for all model variables, outcomes included, with partly completed surveys kept; the amount missing per variable and the missing-at-random assumption are not reported or discussed.

Most outcomes are retrospective self-ratings by the person who rated the exposures, several of them single items or unvalidated counts; the SF-12 and K10 are current and validated, which lowers the concern for those two.

All regression coefficients are printed, but there is no registration, about 130 coefficient tests without correction, and a path model selected by significance and information criteria on the same data.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As evidence that support, preparation, ceremony features or fasting change the ayahuasca experience or mental health, the associations are at very high risk of bias: the central exposures are retrospective ratings of the respondent's own ceremony that overlap in content with the outcomes and can be shaped by them, the sample is self-selected through the organizations whose ceremonies are being rated, and nothing was measured before ayahuasca. The yes-or-no supports and the current mental-health measures (SF-12, K10) are less affected, but their associations remain confounded and small. Cite the paper for what this large self-selected sample reported about ceremony practices, supports and fasting in different contexts (Tables 1 to 3), and, labelled as cross-sectional and self-rated, for the pattern that feeling safe and supported and being offered preparation went with fewer reported difficulties and slightly better current mental health, and that traditional practices, drinking in traditional countries and therapeutic motivation went with more reported extreme fear. Do not cite it for any practice causing or preventing difficult experiences, for the path model as a causal or verified structure, or for effect sizes as clinically meaningful.

key_findings.finding: Of 10,836 survey respondents, the 6,877 who had drunk ayahuasca with two or fewer groups were analysed; of the 6,817 with a known last context, 52.1% (3,553) last drank in an ayahuasca church (UDV, Santo Daime or Barquinha), 19.6% (1,338) with one or more traditional shamans and 28.3% (1,926) in other contexts (non-traditional, mixed, or no guide or ceremony).
key_findings.locator: Materials and Methods › Study Design, 1st paragraph; Demographic and Ayahuasca Drinking Variables, 2nd paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 3, first row

key_findings.finding: Sample by last context (church, traditional, other): women 50.7%, 48.5%, 50.6%; mean age 40.0 (SD 12.8), 40.3 (11.6), 38.4 (11.5); university education 63.2%, 60.4%, 61.3%; living in Brazil 87.0%, 6.4%, 19.4%; any lifetime mental-health diagnosis 29.2%, 39.0%, 44.5% (mean number 0.5, 0.8, 0.9); diagnosed anxiety or depression when drinking 19.5%, 27.1%, 31.5%; years since the last drink 1.2, 1.6, 1.2.
key_findings.note: The F statistic printed for age repeats the one for mental-health diagnoses (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Number of times ayahuasca was drunk, by last context: in the church group 28.3% had drunk 201 to 500 times and 28.5% 500 to 5,000 times, while in the traditional and other groups 18.6% and 19.8% had drunk once, 27.0% and 30.4% two or three times, and 20.4% and 17.8% four or five times.
key_findings.locator: Table 3, number of times drunk rows

key_findings.finding: Motivations (n = 6,818; more than one allowed): increased spiritual awareness, understanding or connection 79.4%; insight into oneself 68.8%; clarity about life purpose or direction 65.2%; dealing with emotional difficulties 37.3%; improving personal relationships 35.0%; general interest in psychedelic medicine or therapy 23.2%; curiosity and adventure 22.7%; intellectual or creative inspiration 21.8%; healing a mental-health condition 21.2%; healing childhood trauma or abuse 16.1%; visual effects 12.8%; healing a physical condition 12.2%; healing adult trauma or abuse 9.1%; just to have the experience 8.8%; grief or loss 8.7%.

Ceremony characteristics at the last context (n = 6,749): live traditional chants or icaros 37.7%; recommended sexual abstinence before ceremonies 34.7%; blowing of smoke for healing and purification 31.8%; smudging 28.7%; other live singing or chanting 22.8%; non-traditional instruments 21.9%; individual blessings 18.5%; recitations such as prayers 18.2%; whistling 16.7%; dance 12.9%; sucking from affected parts of the body 4.6%. Mean ratings (1 to 4): empathy, respect and genuineness of those leading 3.8; emotional and physical safety 3.8; support available during the ceremony 3.8; a powerful and sacred ritual 3.7; chance to discuss history, motivations or concerns beforehand 3.1; guidance beforehand on dealing with possible difficulties 3.1.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, right-hand column: ceremony characteristics, the safety and support score items, and additional supports (the two preparation activities items)

key_findings.finding: By last context (church, traditional, other): mean support-and-safety rating 3.9, 3.8, 3.4; preparation rating 3.1, 3.3, 3.0; religious hymns or sermons 90.0%, 25.3%, 26.0%; mean number of traditional practices 0.2, 3.5, 2.3 and of non-traditional practices 0.3, 1.7, 1.9; religious or spiritual counselling 52.1%, 11.2%, 9.8%; psychologist or psychotherapist 0.8%, 7.1%, 5.8%; yoga or tai-chi 1.7%, 23.6%, 18.3%; fasting 2.0%, 34.9%, 25.7%; mean number of therapeutic motivations 0.5, 1.7, 1.7. By region of most drinking (Brazil, other Latin America, other countries), fasting 2.1%, 37.4%, 26.3%. All differences p < 0.001 except preparation by region (p = 0.001).
key_findings.note: Several F statistics in Table 2 are duplicated across rows and panels (see reporting issues); the percentages and means are unaffected.

key_findings.finding: Ceremony type and place, adjusted B (SE): traditional practices with higher PEQ-S 0.04 (0.01, p = 0.008), lower community closeness −0.16 (0.04), higher K10 0.16 (0.06, p = 0.005) and more PGIC improvement 0.05 (0.02, p = 0.031), not with SF-12 MCS (−0.19, p = 0.090); drinking mostly in a traditional country with lower community closeness −1.35 (0.17) and lower K10 −0.47 (0.22, p = 0.035); non-traditional practices with more self-insights 0.1 (0.03) and higher SIMO 0.77 (0.21), with no final outcome and not with community (0.05, p = 0.252); religious characteristics with stronger community 0.5 (0.11) and lower SIMO −1.04 (0.53, p = 0.050) and PEQ-S −0.08 (0.04, p = 0.039), with no final outcome.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 and Table 5, ceremony characteristics rows; Results › Multivariate Models, 2nd and 5th paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Covariates: the number of times ayahuasca had been drunk went with every final outcome (PWG 1.2 (0.06), SF-12 MCS 0.53 (0.06), K10 −0.24 (0.03), PGIC 0.1 (0.01), all p < 0.001); the number of lifetime mental-health diagnoses with poorer current mental health (SF-12 MCS −1.05 (0.11), K10 0.73 (0.06), both p < 0.001).
key_findings.locator: Table 5, covariates rows; Materials and Methods › Analysis Framework, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Structural model: motivation, ceremony and support variables predicted five intermediate outcomes (self-insights, SIMO, integration difficulties, extreme fear, community closeness), which predicted perceived growth in wellbeing, which in turn predicted current mental health (K10 and SF-12 MCS); integration difficulties also predicted poorer current mental health directly. The legend gives significance levels only; coefficients are in Figure 2 (image) and supplementary Table S1 (not read).
key_findings.locator: Results › Proposed Model, 1st paragraph; Figure 2 legend

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: a non-random, self-selected sample that risks a bias towards people with positive effects; entirely self-report, with several retrospective items (not the SF-12 or K10); no data on mental health before ayahuasca, with the number of lifetime diagnoses used as an imperfect proxy; no data on the composition, purity or dose of the brew; a traditional-country variable that only roughly captures facilitators' skill; and set measured only as motivations, not as state of mind at the time of drinking.

Conclusion: the authors find limited evidence that any one set of practices is superior, and single out tangible and intangible supports that give a sense of safety and support in the ceremony, and preparation activities, as particularly important.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 prints the age comparison as F(2, 5,521) = 97.23, identical to the statistic for the number of lifetime mental-health diagnoses; the age row's group sizes (3,512, 1,329, printed as 1,1329, and 1,919) give 6,757 error df, and the printed means and SDs give F of about 13 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 3, age and lifetime mental-health diagnosis rows
reporting_issues.consequence: A copying error; recomputed, the age difference is still significant (p < 0.001) but small (40.0, 40.3 and 38.4 years). The printed statistic should not be quoted.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 repeats F statistics across different variables and panels: 714.5 for experiential motivation and for non-traditional characteristics by context (both df 2, 6,759) and again for non-traditional characteristics by region (df 2, 6,594); 4680.0 for traditional characteristics by context and by region; 314.1 for the safe-and-supported score by context and by region. The region panel also tests religious characteristics, a percentage, with an F statistic.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least some of these statistics are copying errors and cannot be quoted; the means and percentages differ clearly enough that the differences themselves are not in doubt.

reporting_issues.issue: The number of people behind the PGIC analysis is given three ways: 1,276 in the abstract, 1,278 in Table 5, and 534, 274 and 459 (sum 1,267) in the Table 3 row for prior anxiety or depression, where, unlike every other row, the bracketed numbers appear to be counts of people answering yes rather than the number answering (with 19.5%, 27.1% and 31.5% they imply about 5,206 respondents, close to the N of 5,214 printed for that test; editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Table 3, prior anxiety or depression row; Table 5, PGIC column
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; quote the model n (1,278) with this caveat.

reporting_issues.issue: The discussion departs from the tables twice: it says traditional practices were associated with poorer current mental health on both the SF-12 MCS and the K10, while Table 5 shows only the K10 association (SF-12 MCS B = −0.19, SE 0.11, p = 0.090); and it says non-traditional practices were associated with stronger ayahuasca community, while Table 4 gives B = 0.05, p = 0.252, and the Figure 2 legend lists that path as not significant. The same passage does not mention the association of non-traditional practices with extreme fear (B = 0.1, p = 0.007).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 4th paragraph; Table 4; Table 5; Figure 2 legend
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the tables, not the discussion's summary, for these associations.

reporting_issues.issue: Context percentages (52.1%, 19.6%, 28.3%) are of the 6,817 respondents with a known last context, not of the 6,877 analysed, although the Results call them the full sample; in Table 2 the church share of people who drank mostly in Brazil is 87.55% in one panel and 87.4% in the other, and the chi-squared N for 'other countries' is 6,817 while the other two country rows use 6,621.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 1st paragraph; Table 2; Table 3
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; 60 respondents have no known context and the denominators shift between tables.

reporting_issues.issue: Smaller errors: the PWB-PTCQ is said to measure change in five areas but six are listed; the footnote to Tables 4 and 5 places the lifetime-use categories in Table 1 when they are in Table 3, and two of those categories overlap at 500 (201–500 and 500–5000); model fit is printed as p < 0.000; the companion paper (Perkins et al., 2021) has no journal or DOI in the reference list; the SIMO is cited as Francis (2004) in the text and Francis and Louden (2004) in the references.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Materials and Methods › Mental Health, Wellbeing and Spirituality Variables, 1st and 3rd paragraphs; Tables 3 to 5 and footnotes; References
reporting_issues.consequence: None for the findings; worth knowing when the instruments and the companion paper are traced.

reporting_issues.issue: No mean, SD or distribution is reported for any outcome (extreme fear, integration difficulties, self-insights, SIMO, PEQ-S, community closeness, PWG, SF-12 MCS, K10, PGIC); Tables 1 to 3 describe only the exposures and the sample.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Tables 1 to 5; Materials and Methods › Mental Health, Wellbeing and Spirituality Variables
reporting_issues.consequence: The coefficients cannot be set against the spread of the outcomes: only the published score ranges (fear 0 to 10, K10 10 to 50, SIMO 9 to 90) allow the editors' whole-range arithmetic, and whether a few tenths of a point of fear is a small or a large difference in this sample cannot be judged.
